title: FQHC Language Access: A Health Equity Planning Guide
summary: Build an FQHC language access plan using UDS and EHR data, site-level demand, after-hours coverage, interpretation workflows, written materials.
body_markdown:
###


Start with preferred language by site and service line, interpreter usage by language, after-hours demand, phone and telehealth volume, and staff workarounds. The goal is to find where patient language demand and actual access do not match.


###


Look beyond vendor availability. Track time to active interpretation, how often staff use the approved workflow, where they rely on workarounds, whether translated instructions reach patients, and whether communication problems appear in complaints or follow-up.


###


Much of community health happens outside the long provider visit. Medication questions, referrals, scheduling, lab results, and quick nursing interactions can still affect care. Immediate interpretation makes it easier to cover these moments consistently.


###


Use actual request data to identify when coverage is weakest, then make sure staff have an on-demand option that does not depend on a specific interpreter being available. Opalite supports 150+ languages and dialects through AI and can begin immediately for supported spoken languages.


###


Measure total cost per completed interpreted encounter, including silent time, connection effort, after-hours charges, translation, and documentation. Opalite does not charge for hold time or silent minutes and can combine interpretation with multilingual documentation and document translation.
